newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian chancellor under new fire for poll result.
newsitem.headline: Austrian chancellor under new fire for poll result.

text.p: Chancellor Franz Vranitzky faced new calls for his resignation on Monday after a senior Social Democratic colleague was quoted as saying the party desperately needed new leadership with fresh ideas.

Hannes Swoboda, a leading Social Democrat candidate in what proved to the party to be disastrous European parliamentary elections on October 13, told current affairs magazine Profil Vranitzky should begin paving the way for a hand-over of power.
"That is the duty of the chancellor and I am convinced that is what will happen. I would not want to give a definite date but I would not rule out it happening in 1997," Swoboda said.
He was adding his voice to those of senior Social Democrats past and present who have called on Vranitzky to shoulder responsibility for his party's worst humiliation in Austrian democratic history.

The Social Democrats slumped to second place behind their junior coalition partners, the People's Party, as 50 percent of working class voters turned their backs on Vranitzky and supported the nationalist Freedom Party instead.
Swoboda, whose delegation in the European Parliament lost one of its seven original seats in the poll, urged the Social Democrats to reclaim the political ground to the left-of-centre.

"To reposition the Social Democrats as a party of the left we need a team...of people with new ideas and new ways of tackling problems, not politicians who have been in the business for decades," he said.
Vranitzky and his government colleagues had failed to communicate to an electorate that felt betrayed by higher taxes and deteriorating working conditions, Swoboda argued.
"The aim of Social Democracy is to aid modernisation while preventing it from running amok...We have to help those who are less well paid to cope with the changes," he said.
The party leadership had also lost the ideological debate with the left-leaning Liberals and Greens, who made big inroads among students and intellectuals.

The grand coalition of Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party had grown stale after a decade of rule, Swoboda added. "Party officials should listen to their children, who really don't view the red-black (Social Democrat-conservative) coalition as very attractive," he said.

Swoboda's broadside came as a new public opinion poll showed 55 percent of voters supported Finance Minister Viktor Klima as Vranitzky's successor. Klima remains a favourite with voters despite being the architect of an unpopular austerity budget.
"Viktor Klima is certainly predestined to play a major role...along with (Interior Minister) Caspar Einem," Swoboda said.

Vranitzky and his party manager, Brigitte Ederer, declined to comment on the latest speculation about the chancellor's future. Vranitzky has insisted he will not step down before the next scheduled general election in 1999.
